parts.text: After Jerusalem falls into Nebuchadnezzar’s power, selected young captives are trained for royal service. Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah receive Babylonian names. Daniel resolves not to defile himself with the king’s food and wine and requests a ten-day trial of pulse and water. Their appearance proves better than that of the others, and their requested diet continues.

God gives the four knowledge and skill, while Daniel also receives understanding of visions and dreams. At the end of their training, the king finds none comparable to them, and they enter his service. Their wisdom surpasses that of the kingdom’s magicians and astrologers. Daniel continues into the reign of Cyrus.

chapters.title: The image and the everlasting kingdom

parts.text: Nebuchadnezzar demands that his wise men reveal both his dream and its meaning, threatening death when they cannot. Daniel obtains time and joins his companions in prayer. God reveals the secret in a night vision, and Daniel praises him as the giver of wisdom who appoints and removes kings.

Daniel describes an image with gold, silver, brass, iron, and iron mixed with clay. A stone cut without hands destroys it and grows into a mountain filling the earth. The metals represent successive kingdoms, beginning with Nebuchadnezzar’s, while God establishes a kingdom that cannot be destroyed. Daniel credits God alone with the revelation. The king honors Daniel and appoints his companions over Babylon’s affairs.

Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image and commands everyone to worship when the music sounds, on pain of being burned alive. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego refuse. When challenged, they affirm that God can deliver them but declare that, even if he does not, they will not serve the king’s gods or worship the image.

The furious king orders an intensely heated furnace. The men who throw them in are killed by its flames, but the three walk unbound and unharmed with a fourth figure whom the king describes as like the Son of God. They emerge without even the smell of fire. Nebuchadnezzar blesses their God, condemns speech against him, and promotes the three men.

Nebuchadnezzar recounts a dream of a vast tree cut down by heavenly command, leaving a protected stump. Daniel explains that the king will be driven from human society and live with beasts for seven times until he acknowledges that the Most High rules human kingdoms. The preserved stump means his kingdom will be restored. Daniel urges righteousness and mercy to the poor.

Twelve months later, the king boasts of Babylon as his own achievement, and the warning is fulfilled. He lives like an animal until he lifts his eyes to heaven and his understanding returns. His honor and kingdom are restored. He concludes by praising the King of heaven, whose works are true and who is able to humble those walking in pride.

Belshazzar holds a feast and uses vessels taken from Jerusalem’s temple while praising lifeless gods. A hand writes on the wall, terrifying him. His wise men cannot explain the writing, so the queen recalls Daniel’s wisdom. The king offers Daniel honors and authority if he can interpret it.

Daniel refuses to bargain for rewards and reminds Belshazzar that he knew how God humbled Nebuchadnezzar but did not humble himself. The writing declares his kingdom numbered and finished, himself weighed and found wanting, and his kingdom divided to the Medes and Persians. Daniel receives the announced honors, but that same night Belshazzar is killed and Darius the Median takes the kingdom.

Daniel’s integrity prevents jealous officials from finding grounds against him, so they persuade Darius to forbid petitions to anyone except the king for thirty days. Daniel continues praying to God as before. His enemies report him, and the king cannot undo the decree despite his efforts to save him.

Daniel is placed in the lions’ den and sealed inside. After a sleepless night, Darius hurries there and finds him alive: God sent an angel to shut the lions’ mouths. Daniel is lifted out unharmed because he trusted God. His accusers and their families are cast into the den, and Darius commands reverence for Daniel’s living God, whose kingdom endures forever.

chapters.title: Four beasts and the heavenly judgment

parts.text: Daniel sees four beasts rise from a troubled sea, the last terrifying and bearing ten horns. A smaller horn rises, displaces three others, and speaks boastfully. The Ancient of days sits in judgment, and the fourth beast is destroyed. One like the Son of man comes with heaven’s clouds and receives an everlasting kingdom embracing all peoples.

An attendant explains that the beasts represent kings and that the saints will possess the kingdom. The fourth kingdom’s horns represent kings, including one who persecutes the saints and seeks to change times and laws. His allotted period ends in judgment, and his dominion is taken away. The kingdom is given to the saints of the Most High, while Daniel remains troubled by the vision.

chapters.title: The ram, goat, and fierce king

parts.text: Daniel sees a two-horned ram overcome by a goat from the west. The goat’s great horn breaks and four horns replace it. A smaller horn grows powerful, attacks the host and sanctuary, removes the daily sacrifice, and casts truth down. Daniel hears that the sanctuary will be cleansed after 2,300 days.

Gabriel identifies the ram with Media and Persia and the goat with Grecia. Its great horn is the first king; four kingdoms follow his broken rule. A fierce ruler later destroys through power and deceit, opposing even the Prince of princes, but is broken without human hand. Daniel is told to preserve the vision, which concerns many days ahead, and is left sick and astonished.

Reading Jeremiah, Daniel understands the seventy years appointed for Jerusalem’s desolations and seeks God with prayer and fasting. He confesses Israel’s rebellion, including its refusal to hear the prophets, and acknowledges the justice of the disaster foretold in Moses’ law. He pleads for Jerusalem and the sanctuary, appealing to God’s mercy and name rather than the people’s righteousness.

Gabriel arrives while Daniel prays and announces seventy weeks concerning his people and holy city. The message describes Jerusalem’s rebuilding, Messiah the Prince, Messiah being cut off, and destruction of the city and sanctuary. A final week includes a covenant with many, the cessation of sacrifice in its midst, and desolation until the determined end. The passage links these events with God’s purposes of reconciliation and everlasting righteousness.

After three weeks of mourning and restricted food, Daniel sees a radiant man beside the river Hiddekel. His companions flee in fear, while Daniel loses his strength and falls down. A messenger raises him and says his prayer was heard from the first day, but the prince of Persia resisted for twenty-one days until Michael came to help. The message concerns what will happen to Daniel’s people in the latter days.

Daniel is overwhelmed and unable to speak until touched and strengthened. He is assured that he is greatly beloved and told not to fear. The messenger prepares to disclose the scripture of truth before returning to the conflict involving Persia and Grecia, with Michael identified as Daniel’s people’s prince.

chapters.title: Conflicting kingdoms and an appointed end

parts.text: The revelation describes Persian kings, a mighty ruler whose kingdom divides four ways, and repeated struggles between kings of the north and south. Alliances through marriage fail, armies invade and retreat, and rulers gain power only to fall. The account traces changing fortunes rather than an uninterrupted triumph for either side.

A contemptible ruler gains authority through flattery and deceit. Forces profane the sanctuary, remove the daily sacrifice, and establish the abomination of desolation. Those who know God resist, while the understanding teach many and suffer persecution that refines them. A self-exalting king speaks against God and prospers only until the appointed indignation is complete. Further warfare reaches the glorious land and Egypt, but the ruler finally meets his end without help.

chapters.title: Trouble, resurrection, and the sealed words

parts.text: Michael stands for Daniel’s people during an unparalleled time of trouble. Those written in the book are delivered. Many sleeping in the earth’s dust awake, some to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting contempt. The wise and those who turn others to righteousness shine gloriously. Daniel is told to seal the book until the time of the end.

A heavenly oath gives a time, times, and half a time and connects completion with the scattering of the holy people’s power. Daniel still asks for understanding. The answer speaks of purification, 1,290 days from the removal of sacrifice and establishment of the abomination, and blessing for reaching 1,335 days. Daniel is promised rest and his appointed place at the end.
